A murder whose perpetrator is unknown (verses 1–9)

When a murderer could not be identified, Israel was commanded to carry out a solemn ceremony acknowledging and removing the guilt from the land.

This demonstrated the deep horror with which God regarded murder.

His providence has often brought such hidden works of darkness to light.

The guilty person's sin has sometimes been revealed in unexpected ways.

Everyone should recognize the seriousness of murder and help prevent, investigate and punish it lawfully.

The elders solemnly declared that they had neither committed the murder nor helped it take place.

The priests prayed for the country and its people, asking God to show mercy.

Our prayers should seek to counter the evil with which others are filling the world.

We should learn to prevent, detect and oppose murder diligently.

We must also avoid becoming involved in other people's sins.

If we refuse to speak against fruitless works of darkness, we risk sharing in them.

A soldier and a captive woman (verses 10–14)

The law permitted an Israelite soldier, in certain circumstances, to marry a captive woman if he wished.

Henry emphasizes that allowing such a marriage did not mean approving of it.

The rule also revealed how strongly justice and honor should govern marriage, which is a sacred commitment.

The rights of the firstborn (verses 15–17)

A father was forbidden to disinherit his eldest son without just cause merely because he preferred another child.

This principle concerning children remains binding on parents.

They must give each child the rights that belong to them, without favoritism.

The stubborn and rebellious son (verses 18–21)

Notice how the offender is described.

He is stubborn and rebellious.

A child was not to be punished for limited understanding, slow learning or lack of intelligence.

The problem was deliberate refusal to obey.

Nothing draws people toward sin and makes them more obstinate than drunkenness.

People ruled by drinking forget their duty to honor their parents.

Both the father and mother were required to bring the complaint before the city's elders.

Children who deliberately reject their responsibilities should not blame their parents if affection eventually grows strained.

Under Israel's ancient law, the offender was to be publicly stoned.

Henry sees the punishment as showing the seriousness of persistent contempt for parental authority.

Though this offense does not receive that civil punishment in his own day, it remains offensive to God.

When young people become enslaved early to bodily appetite, the heart hardens and conscience loses its sensitivity.

Such a course leads toward rebellion and ruin.

The body of someone executed must be removed (verses 22 and 23)

Under the law of Moses, contact with a dead body made a person ceremonially unclean.

An executed person's body therefore could not be left hanging overnight, defiling the land.

This rule has a special connection with Christ.

Someone left hanging in such disgrace was described as cursed by God.

Henry explains that this language expressed the deepest humiliation: the person appeared rejected by both heaven and earth.

Moses used those words under the Spirit's guidance so that they could later be applied to Christ.

Through his death on the cross, Jesus endured the law's curse for us.

That reveals his love and invites us to trust him.

(15-17)

Malefactors not to be left hanging all night. | (22-23) |
Verses 1-9
If a murderer could not be found out, great solemnity is provided for putting away the guilt from the land, as an expression of dread and detesting of that sin. The providence of God has often wonderfully brought to light these hidden works of darkness, and the sin of the guilty has often strangely found them out. The dread of murder should be deeply impressed upon every heart, and all should join in detecting and punishing those who are guilty. The elders were to profess that they had not been any way aiding or abetting the sin. The priests were to pray to God for the country and nation, that God would be merciful. We must empty that measure by our prayers, which others are filling by their sins. All would be taught by this solemnity, to use the utmost care and diligence to prevent, discover, and punish murder. We may all learn from hence to take heed of partaking in other men's sins. And we have fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, if we do not reprove them.
[Deut.21.10-Deut.21.14]
Verses 10-14
By this law a soldier was allowed to marry his captive, if he pleased. This might take place upon some occasions; but the law does not show any approval of it. It also intimates how binding the laws of justice and honour are in marriage; which is a sacred engagement.
[Deut.21.15-Deut.21.17]
Verses 15-17
This law restrains men from disinheriting their eldest sons without just cause. The principle in this case as to children, is still binding to parents; they must give children their right without partiality.
[Deut.21.18-Deut.21.21]
Verses 18-21
Observe how the criminal is here described. He is a stubborn and rebellious son. No child was to fare the worse for weakness of capacity, slowness, or dulness, but for wilfulness and obstinacy. Nothing draws men into all manner of wickedness, and hardens them in it more certainly and fatally, than drunkenness. When men take to drinking, they forget the law of honouring parents. His own father and mother must complain of him to the elders of the city. Children who forget their duty, must thank themselves, and not blame their parents, if they are regarded with less and less affection. He must be publicly stoned to death by the men of his city. Disobedience to a parent's authority must be very evil, when such a punishment was ordered; nor is it less provoking to God now, though it escapes punishment in this world. But when young people early become slaves to sensual appetites, the heart soon grows hard, and the conscience callous; and we can expect nothing but rebellion and destruction.
[Deut.21.22-Deut.21.23]
Verses 22-23
By the law of Moses, the touch of a dead body was defiling, therefore dead bodies must not be left hanging, as that would defile the land. There is one reason here which has reference to Christ; "He that is hanged is accursed of God;" that is, it is the highest degree of disgrace and reproach. Those who see a man thus hanging between heaven and earth, will conclude him abandoned of both, and unworthy of either. Moses, by the Spirit, uses this phrase of being accursed of God, when he means no more than being treated most disgracefully, that it might afterward be applied to the death of Christ, and might show that in it he underwent the curse of the law for us; which proves his love, and encourages to faith in him.

Neighborly kindness (verses 1–4)

If we consistently followed the rule of treating others as we would want them to treat us, many more detailed commandments would become unnecessary.

Finding an object that belongs to someone else never makes it our own property.

True religion teaches us to be good neighbors.

We should willingly do good and offer practical assistance to everyone.

We cannot know how soon we may need someone else's help.

Instructions for everyday conduct (verses 5–12)

God's providence extends to even the smallest details of life, and his commands teach us to honor him in those details.

We live under his care and watchful eye.

Some instructions may seem minor.

But because they belong to God's law, they concern matters of real importance.

If we want to show that we are his people, we must value his will and glory above the meaningless fashions of the world.

Even when choosing clothing, just as when eating or drinking, we should take care to preserve the purity of our own hearts and actions and avoid harming others.

Our purpose should be clear, our hearts sincere, and our conduct consistent in every part of life.

Laws concerning sexual purity (verses 13–30)

These and related regulations may have been necessary for Israel's historical circumstances.

But Henry says there is no need for Christians to investigate every difficult detail with undue curiosity.

Their continuing moral meaning is connected with the seventh commandment.

They restrain bodily lusts, which fight against the soul.

Those excluded from Israel's assembly (verses 1–8)

We should value the privileges of belonging to God's people, for ourselves and for our children, above every other advantage.

Under the gospel, no bodily defect, ancestor's offense or difference in nationality bars someone from the church's spiritual blessings.

But a corrupt heart can keep us from enjoying those blessings.

And the bad example of parents—or marriages that draw a family away from faith—can keep children from seeking them.

Cleanliness in Israel's camp (verses 9–14)

Nothing offensive or unclean was to be tolerated in the Lord's camp.

If Israel had to pay careful attention to the cleanliness of the body, how much more should we preserve purity of heart and mind!

The runaway servant, lending, vows and everyday generosity (verses 15–25)

It is honorable to shelter and protect someone vulnerable, provided the person is not deliberately engaged in wrongdoing.

People who convert to the truth should be treated with particular tenderness, so that they are not drawn back to worldly life.

We cannot honor God with our possessions unless we acquired them honestly.

What matters is not only what we give, but how we obtained it.

Where someone borrows money to engage in an activity that brings or may bring profit, Henry considers it just for the lender to share in that gain.

But people who borrow simply to obtain necessary food should be treated with compassion.

A solemn promise deliberately spoken must be fulfilled completely.

Israelites were allowed to pick and eat grapes or grain along their journey, but they were forbidden to carry any away.

This arrangement showed the abundant food Canaan would provide and made provision for poor travelers.

We should be similarly generous and hospitable, willing to give without treating every gift as a loss.

Yet we must not exploit the generosity of others or use permitted privileges as a way to take more than is right.

Faithfulness in our commitments and respect for other people's property should characterize God's people.

The camp of the Lord must have nothing offensive in it. If there must be this care taken to preserve the body clean, much more should we be careful to keep the mind pure.
[Deut.23.15-Deut.23.25]
Verses 15-25
It is honourable to shelter and protect the weak, provided they are not wicked. Proselytes and converts to the truth, should be treated with particular tenderness, that they may have no temptation to return to the world. We cannot honour God with our substance, unless it be honestly and honourably come by. It must not only be considered what we give, but how we got it. Where the borrower gets, or hopes to get, it is just that the lender should share the gain; but to him that borrows for necessary food, pity must be showed. That which is gone out of thy lips, as a solemn and deliberate vow, must not be recalled, but thou shalt keep and perform it punctually and fully. They were allowed to pluck and eat of the corn or grapes that grew by the road side; only they must not carry any away. This law intimated what great plenty of corn and wine they should have in Canaan. It provided for the support of poor travellers, and teaches us to be kind to such, teaches us to be ready to distribute, and not to think every thing lost that is given away. Yet it forbids us to abuse the kindness of friends, or to take advantage of what is allowed. Faithfulness to their engagements should mark the people of God; and they should never encroach upon others.

Divorce and the responsibility to bear hardship (verses 1–4)

Sometimes God's providence, or a person's own unwise choice in marriage, brings a Christian into a painful relationship rather than the companionship hoped for.

Such a person should sincerely prefer to bear the cross rather than seek a form of relief that leads toward sin, disorder and suffering.

God's grace can make that burden holy, sustain the person under it and teach conduct that gradually makes the situation more bearable.

Marriage, kidnapping and consideration for debtors (verses 5–13)

It is of great importance that love between a husband and wife be preserved.

Both should carefully avoid whatever might cause them to become distant or estranged from each other.

Kidnapping people and enslaving them was a capital crime, not an ordinary theft whose wrong could be settled merely by restitution.

The laws concerning leprosy also had to be followed carefully.

When we recognize guilt and fear God's judgment, we should not conceal the truth or try to shake off our convictions.

Instead, through repentance, prayer and humble confession, we should seek the path of forgiveness and peace.

God also gave regulations about the possessions a lender could hold as security for a loan.

We should consider another person's necessities and comfort as seriously as our own financial advantage.

Let a poor debtor keep the garment needed for sleeping and thank God for your kindness.

Debtors should recognize the generosity of creditors who refuse to take every legal advantage available to them.

Such restraint should not be regarded as weakness.

Justice and generosity toward those in need (verses 14–22)

Purity, reverence for God, justice, mercy, fair dealing, kindness to poor and vulnerable people, consideration for their needs and generosity of spirit are plainly pleasing to God.

These virtues are appropriate for everyone he has redeemed.

The difficulty lies not in proving their value, but in putting them consistently into practice in our everyday conduct.

The custom regulated here seems to have been established under Jewish law to keep family inheritances distinct.

Offering the firstfruits with grateful remembrance (verses 1–11)

When God fulfills his promises to us, he expects us to acknowledge the fulfillment and give him the honor for his faithfulness.

The comforts we receive through created things become doubly pleasant when we recognize that they flow from his promises.

A person bringing firstfruits was to remember the humble beginnings of the nation.

“My father was a Syrian who was about to perish.”

Moses describes Jacob as a Syrian.

Israel's ancestors had gone to live in Egypt as foreigners.

There they became enslaved.

They were once poor, despised and oppressed.

Even after becoming wealthy and powerful, the people had no reason for pride, self-confidence or forgetfulness of God.

Their offering should express heartfelt gratitude for the Lord's goodness to Israel.

The comfort we enjoy privately should make us grateful for public peace and abundant provision too.

Present blessings should call to mind mercies received long ago and those still promised for the future.

The worshiper brought the basket of firstfruits before God.

Whatever good gift we receive, he wants us to enjoy it gratefully, recognizing him as the source of every comfort.

Prayer after the third-year tithe (verses 12–15)

Even if the land produces an abundant harvest, it will give little true satisfaction unless God also adds his blessing.

This ceremony pictured the relationship between God, reconciled to his people, and each genuine believer.

It displayed the privileges and duties that belong to this relationship.

Under the covenant of grace in Jesus Christ, we should watch carefully over our lives.

We ought to show by our conduct that the Lord is our God and we are his people, while waiting in the way he appointed for the complete fulfillment of his generous promises.

The covenant and wholehearted obedience (verses 16–19)

Moses urged Israel to obey God's commands for the very purpose for which they were given.

They are the Lord's laws: do them.

Do not merely argue about them or turn away after hearing them.

Do not carry them out carelessly or hypocritically.

Obey with your whole heart and soul.

If we have professed to take the Lord as our God but refuse to follow his commandments, we have broken a sacred commitment.

We were chosen for obedience (1 Peter 1:2).

We were chosen to be holy (Ephesians 1:4).

We have been purified to become God's special people, eager not only to do good works but to devote ourselves zealously to them (Titus 2:14).

Holiness is true honor.

It is also the only path to everlasting honor.

God's law and the altar of uncut stone (verses 1–10)

As soon as Israel entered Canaan, the people were to erect a monument on which God's law would be written.

They were also to build an altar.

God's word and prayer belong together.

Israelites were not free to set up other altars wherever they pleased.

But God could command one for a particular occasion.

The altar was to be built from rough, uncut stones found in the field.

Christ, our Altar, is the Stone cut from the mountain without human hands.

He was rejected by the builders as lacking outward beauty, yet God the Father accepted him and made him the chief cornerstone.

The Old Testament's written law carries a curse against transgression.

That curse would terrify us if the New Testament did not also reveal an altar—Christ—to console and save us.

Printed copies of Scripture now spare us from the need to write its words publicly in the particular manner Israel was commanded.

The purpose of gospel ministry should be to make God's word as clear as possible.

Yet even the clearest preaching cannot make us wise for salvation unless the Holy Spirit gives it saving power.

We should therefore pray continually and earnestly for the Spirit's work.

The curses announced on Mount Ebal (verses 11–26)

The six tribes assigned to pronounce blessings descended from the free women.

Henry relates this to the promise belonging to the free woman in Galatians 4:31.

Levi was included among the tribes.

Ministers should apply God's warnings and promises first to their own consciences.

They should agree with faith-filled Amen to what they announce to others.

They must encourage people through promised blessings and also warn them through the threatened curse.

Every curse was met with an Amen from the people.

That meant they accepted that God truly judges the ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings.

They also acknowledged that those who commit such wrongs deserve his judgment.

The final curse reached beyond the particular offenses named.

It included everyone who fails to carry out the whole law.

Not only committing the evil the law forbids but also neglecting the good the law commands brings guilt.

Without Christ's atoning blood, sinners cannot enjoy fellowship with a holy God or offer him anything truly acceptable.

God's righteous law condemns whoever breaks it, however briefly or in whatever way.

We remain under its curse until Christ's redemption is applied to our hearts.

Saving grace also teaches believers to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live with self-control, righteousness and reverence for God in the present world.

Such people assent to God's law and delight in it inwardly.

The truly holy life is the place where solid joy and genuine peace are found.

As soon as they were come into Canaan, they must set up a monument, on which they must write the words of this law. They must set up an altar. The word and prayer must go together. Though they might not, of their own heads, set up any altar besides that at the tabernacle; yet, by the appointment of God, they might, upon special occasion. This altar must be made of unhewn stones, such as they found upon the field. Blessed be God, the printed copies of the Scriptures among us, do away the necessity of such methods as were presented to Israel. The end of the gospel ministry is, and the end of preachers ought to be, to make the word of God as plain as possible. Yet, unless the Spirit of God prosper such labours with Divine power, we shall not, even by these means, be made wise unto salvation: for this blessing we should therefore daily and earnestly pray.

Ministers should apply to themselves the blessing and curse they preach to others, and by faith set their own Amen to it. And they must not only allure people to their duty with the promises of a blessing, but awe them with the threatenings of a curse, by declaring that a curse would be upon those who do such things. To each of the curses the people were to say, Amen. It professed their faith, that these, and the like curses, were real declarations of the wrath of God against the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, not one jot of which shall fall to the ground. It was acknowledging the equity of these curses. Those who do such things deserve to fall, and lie under the curse. Not only those who do the evil which the law forbids, but those also who omit the good which the law requires. Without the atoning blood of Christ, sinners can neither have communion with a holy God, nor do any thing acceptable to him; his righteous law condemns every one who, at any time, or in any thing, transgresses it. Under its awful curse we remain as transgressors, until the redemption of Christ is applied to our hearts. Wherever the grace of God brings salvation, it teaches the believer to deny ungodliness and wordly lusts, to live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world, consenting to, and delighting in the words of God's law, after the inward man. The blessings promised for obedience (verses 1–14)

This long chapter develops two words: blessing and curse.

Both refer to real conditions with real consequences.

The blessings are described first.

God is slow to become angry and quick to show mercy.

He delights to bless.

It is better to be attracted to goodness by the hope of God's favor, as children who trust their Father, than to be driven to obedience merely through the fear of slaves.

The promised blessing depended upon Israel's careful attention to God's voice.

If the people maintained both the outward form and inward reality of religion within their families and nation, God's providence would prosper their earthly affairs.

The curses associated with disobedience (verses 15–44)

Those who refuse God's commands not only lose the promised blessing but also place themselves under the curse.

The blessing includes true happiness; the curse brings misery.

Notice that the curse is just.

It does not come without reason or for a trivial offense.

Notice also its range and power.

Wherever the sinner travels, God's judgment follows.

Every possession and comfort becomes affected by the curse.

Earthly pleasures can turn bitter when God's anger is joined with them.

No genuine comfort remains.

Moses described many judgments that would come upon the Jewish people because of apostasy and disobedience.

Henry interprets them in light of what he believed had already happened to the Jewish people in his own day.

The final misery described includes loss of hope and comfort, leaving people close to despair.

People who live only by what they see, rather than by faith, risk losing even their sound judgment when the world around them becomes frightening.

Israel's ruin and the curse's final meaning (verses 45–68)

Consider how terrible the calamities can be when God brings judgment even in this life.

Yet these earthly sufferings are only the beginning of sorrows for those who remain under his curse.

What then will be the suffering of the place where the worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished?

Henry finds something astonishing in the history of Israel.

He describes a nation formerly favored by God as later rejected and scattered among other nations while retaining a distinct identity.

He cites the Babylonian exile, the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and later prohibitions on Jewish access to Jerusalem as fulfillments of the warnings.

These are Henry's historical and theological interpretations, retained as part of the commentary rather than new editorial judgments about Jewish people today.

He contrasts Israel's refusal to serve God joyfully with the prospect of being made to serve enemies.

Everyone will finally recognize God's greatness, willingly or under judgment.

Henry highlights the predicted loss of the land (verse 63), bodily rest (verse 65) and even peace of mind.

He observes repeated migrations, banishments and returns.

He considers the correspondence between these historical events and Mosaic prophecy evidence of Scripture's truth.

He also anticipates a future conversion of Jewish people to Christ.

He expects this to precede a wider spread of Christianity among the nations.

This, again, is Henry's reading of the prophecies, not an independent new historical claim.

Moses, speaking through God's Spirit, warned sinners before their ruin.

Such warning gives people an opportunity to repent in time, and leaves them without excuse if they refuse.

Let us be thankful that Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us.

He bore in his own person the judgment our sins deserve—judgment that otherwise would have remained upon us forever.

Let sinners flee to him for refuge.

Let believers rejoice and serve their reconciled God wholeheartedly, grateful for the abundance of his spiritual blessings.

Verses 1-14
This chapter is a very large exposition of two words, the blessing and the curse. They are real things and have real effects. The blessings are here put before the curses. God is slow to anger, but swift to show mercy. It is his delight to bless. It is better that we should be drawn to what is good by a child-like hope of God's favour, than that we be frightened to it by a slavish fear of his wrath. The blessing is promised, upon condition that they diligently hearken to the voice of God. Let them keep up religion, the form and power of it, in their families and nation, then the providence of God would prosper all their outward concerns.
[Deut.28.15-Deut.28.44]
Verses 15-44
If we do not keep God's commandments, we not only come short of the blessing promised, but we lay ourselves under the curse, which includes all misery, as the blessing all happiness. Observe the justice of this curse. It is not a curse causeless, or for some light cause. The extent and power of this curse. Wherever the sinner goes, the curse of God follows; wherever he is, it rests upon him. Whatever he has is under a curse. All his enjoyments are made bitter; he cannot take any true comfort in them, for the wrath of God mixes itself with them. Many judgments are here stated, which would be the fruits of the curse, and with which God would punish the people of the Jews, for their apostacy and disobedience. We may observe the fulfilling of these threatenings in their present state. To complete their misery, it is threatened that by these troubles they should be bereaved of all comfort and hope, and left to utter despair. Those who walk by sight, and not by faith, are in danger of losing reason itself, when every thing about them looks frightful.
[Deut.28.45-Deut.28.68]
Verses 45-68
If God inflicts vengeance, what miseries his curse can bring upon mankind, even in this present world! Yet these are but the beginning of sorrows to those under the curse of God. What then will be the misery of that world where their worm dieth not, and their fire is not quenched! Observe what is here said of the wrath of God, which should come and remain upon the Israelites for their sins. It is amazing to think that a people so long the favourites of Heaven, should be so cast off; and yet that a people so scattered in all nations should be kept distinct, and not mixed with others. If they would not serve God with cheerfulness, they should be compelled to serve their enemies. We may justly expect from God, that if we do not fear his fearful name, we shall feel his fearful plagues; for one way or other God will be feared. The destruction threatened is described. They have, indeed, been plucked from off the land, ver. #(63). Not only by the Babylonish captivity, and when Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans; but afterwards, when they were forbidden to set foot in Jerusalem. They should have no rest; no rest of body, ver. 65, but be continually on the remove, either in hope of gain, or fear of persecution. No rest of the mind, which is much worse. They have been banished from city to city, from country to country; recalled, and banished again. These events, compared with the favour shown to Israel in ancient times, and with the prophecies about them, should not only excite astonishment, but turn unto us for a testimony, assuring us of the truth of Scripture. And when the other prophecies of their conversion to Christ shall come to pass, the whole will be a sign and a wonder to all the nations of the earth, and the forerunner of a general spread of true christianity. The fulfilling of these prophecies upon the Jewish nation, delivered more than three thousand years ago, shows that Moses spake by the Spirit of God; who not only foresees the ruin of sinners, but warns of it, that they may prevent it by a true and timely repentance, or else be left without excuse. And let us be thankful that Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, by being made a curse for us, and bearing in his own person all that punishment which our sins merit, and which we must otherwise have endured for ever. To this Refuge and salvation let sinners flee; therein let believers rejoice, and serve their reconciled God with gladness of heart, for the abundance of his spiritual blessings.

Remembering past and present mercies (verses 1–9)

God's former kindnesses and his recent acts of mercy should both encourage us to obey him.

Hearing ears, seeing eyes and understanding hearts are gifts from the Lord.

Everyone who possesses them owes them to him.

God gives food, clothing, wealth and considerable possessions to many people whom he has not given saving grace.

Many enjoy the gifts without recognizing their Giver, or understanding their proper purpose.

Gratitude and wise self-interest, as well as faithful duty, therefore call us to keep the words of God's covenant.

The danger of self-confidence while sinning (verses 10–21)

The national covenant made with Israel pictured the covenant of grace with genuine believers.

It also represented the outward administration of religion under the gospel.

People who have consented to Christ's new covenant of mercy, and have dedicated themselves to be God's people, should take every opportunity to renew the public confession of their relationship to him.

Their lives should match that confession.

The sinner described here first turns away from God in the heart.

This is where the trouble begins.

Unbelief leads people to abandon the living God for lifeless idols.

The same temptation exists today.

People are drawn away by their own sinful desires and imagination.

Henry describes them as roots growing poisonous plants.

If not stopped, those weeds spread through an entire field.

Satan may disguise the bitterness of sin for a time.

But its true character will become clear, if not sooner, at the final judgment.

The presumptuous sinner hears God's warnings and still assumes there is no danger.

The threats in this passage are among the most serious in Scripture.

If only people who deliberately persist in wrongdoing would read them and tremble.

They are true declarations of God's anger against human ungodliness and injustice.

The danger of national idolatry (verses 22–28)

Moses warned that idolatry would destroy Israel as a nation.

God has sometimes brought ruin upon communities that claimed to be especially close to him.

He does not do so without just reason.

We should seek to recognize that reason, give glory to God for his justice and take warning ourselves.

The law of Moses leaves sinners under its curse and expelled from the Lord's land.

But through Christ's grace, sinners who repent and believe are planted again into his favor.

God's power then protects them from finally being torn away.

The revealed and hidden things of God (verse 29)

Moses ended his prophecy of Israel's rejection in a way comparable to Paul's conclusion on the same subject (Romans 11:33).

We are not meant to pry into God's secret purposes or claim certainty about what he has not revealed.

But we are commanded and encouraged to study diligently what he has revealed.

He has withheld nothing necessary or truly profitable for us.

Only what is good for us not to know remains hidden.

The aim of divine revelation is not to provide endless material for curious speculation or argument.

It is to enable us to obey God's law and receive his blessing.

Scripture plainly reveals what is needed for that purpose.

Going beyond it will not help us.

Through the light God has given, we may live and die in peace and finally be happy forever.

The national covenant made with Israel, not only typified the covenant of grace made with true believers, but also represented the outward dispensation of the gospel. Those who have been enabled to consent to the Lord's new covenant of mercy and grace in Jesus Christ, and to give up themselves to be his people, should embrace every opportunity of renewing their open profession of relation to him, and their obligation to him, as the God of salvation, walking according thereto. The sinner is described as one whose heart turns away from his God; there the mischief begins, in the evil heart of unbelief, which inclines men to depart from the living God to dead idols. Even to this sin men are now tempted, when drawn aside by their own lusts and fancies. Such men are roots that bear gall and wormwood. They are weeds which, if let alone, overspread the whole field. Satan may for a time disguise this bitter morsel, so that thou shalt not have the natural taste of it, but at the last day, if not before, the true taste shall be discerned. Notice the sinner's security in sin. Though he hears the words of the curse, yet even then he thinks himself safe from the wrath of God. There is scarcely a threatening in all the book of God more dreadful than this. Oh that presumptuous sinners would read it, and tremble! for it is a real declaration of the wrath of God, against ungodliness and unrighteousness of man.
[Deut.29.22-Deut.29.28]
Verses 22-28
Idolatry would be the ruin of their nation. It is no new thing for God to bring desolating judgments on a people near to him in profession. He never does this without good reason. It concerns us to seek for the reason, that we may give glory to God, and take warning to ourselves. Thus the law of Moses leaves sinners under the curse, and rooted out of the Lord's land; but the grace of Christ toward penitent, believing sinners, plants them again in their land; and they shall no more be pulled up, being kept by the power of God.
[Deut.29.29]
Verse 29
Moses ends his prophecy of the Jews' rejection, just as St. Paul ends his discourse on the same subject, when it began to be fulfilled, [Rom.11.33] Ro 11:33. We are forbidden curiously to inquire into the secret counsels of God, and to determine concerning them. But we are directed and encouraged, diligently to seek into that which God has made known. He has kept back nothing that is profitable for us, but only that of which it is good for us to be ignorant. The end of all Divine revelation is, not to furnish curious subjects of speculation and discourse, but that we may do all the words of this law, and be blessed in our deed. This, the Bible plainly reveals; further than this, man cannot profitably go. By this light he may live and die comfortably, and be happy for ever.

Mercy promised to people who return (verses 1–10)

Henry sees here a promise of mercy for Israel in the latter days.

He connects these verses with the warnings given in the previous two chapters and interprets their fulfillment through the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and Israel's long dispersion.

He also understands them as promising a future event that had not yet taken place in his time.

He expects Jewish people to be converted to faith in Christ.

Many interpreters, he notes, also expect a later return to the land of Canaan.

This is Henry's interpretation of prophecy, faithfully reported rather than newly asserted as an established prediction by the editor.

The language of this chapter is, in large part, unconditional promise rather than merely a conditional offer.

The Lord himself promises to circumcise the people's hearts.

When regenerating grace removes corruption and divine love replaces love of sin, people truly repent, turn to God and obey him.

The Lord then delights in doing good to them.

Their change is not merely outward or a change in opinions.

It reaches into their hearts.

It produces hatred of sin and wholehearted love for God, reconciled to them through Jesus Christ.

The people Henry wrote about were far from that condition.

But so were the people who helped kill Jesus before they were converted in one hour on the day of Pentecost.

In the day of God's power, a nation can be born in a day.

He will fulfill his purpose at his own time.

As a conditional promise, the passage also applies to individuals and peoples everywhere.

Even the worst sinners who repent and are converted will receive pardon and be restored to God's favor.

The command is near (verses 11–14)

God's command is not too high for ordinary people to understand.

Its meaning is not reserved for scholars.

It has been written plainly, so that even someone passing by can read it.

It is in people's mouths, in their ordinary language, available for reading and discussion with their children.

It has been made accessible even to those with little education.

This is especially true of the gospel of Christ, to which the apostle Paul applies these words.

God's word is close to us—and Christ is revealed in that word.

If we believe in our hearts that Jesus is the promised Messiah, and openly confess that faith with our mouths, we have Christ with us.

Life and death are set before the people (verses 15–20)

What appeal could be more moving or leave a deeper impression?

Everyone desires life, goodness and happiness, and hopes to escape death, evil and misery.

The Lord has shown great compassion by revealing through his word the path that leads to everlasting happiness.

If people refuse that path, the fault is theirs.

The matter can be stated simply.

Love and serve God, and you will find life and happiness.

Turn away from him, reject his service and follow false gods, and you will bring ruin on yourselves.

Since humanity's fall, there has never been more than one way to heaven.

The Old and New Testaments reveal the same way, although the New Testament makes it clearer.

Moses spoke of the same way of being accepted by God that Paul later explained more fully.

Paul spoke of the same obedience that Moses had expounded in greater detail.

Both Testaments bring the true and good way close to us and make it known.

[Deut.30.1-Deut.30.10]
Chapter 30
Chapter Outline
Mercies promised to the repentant. | (1-10) |
The commandment manifest. | (11-14) |
Death and life set before them. | (15-20) |
Verses 1-10
In this chapter is a plain intimation of the mercy God has in store for Israel in the latter days. This passage refers to the prophetic warnings of the last two chapters, which have been mainly fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, and in their dispersion to the present day; and there can be no doubt that the prophetic promise contained in these verses yet remain to come to pass. The Jewish nation shall in some future period, perhaps not very distant, be converted to the faith of Christ; and, many think, again settled in the land of Canaan. The language here used is in a great measure absolute promises; not merely a conditional engagement, but declaring an event assuredly to take place. For the Lord himself here engages to "circumcise their hearts;" and when regenerating grace has removed corrupt nature, and Divine love has supplanted the love of sin, they certainly will reflect, repent, return to God, and obey him; and he will rejoice in doing them good. The change that will be wrought upon them will not be only outward, or consisting in mere opinions; it will reach to their souls. It will produce in them an utter hatred of all sin, and a fervent love to God, as their reconciled God in Christ Jesus; they will love him with all their hearts, and with all their soul. They are very far from this state of mind at present, but so were the murderers of the Lord Jesus, on the day of Pentecost; who yet in one hour were converted unto God. So shall it be in the day of God's power; a nation shall be born in a day; the Lord will hasten it in his time. As a conditional promise this passage belongs to all persons and all people, not to Israel only; it assures us that the greatest sinners, if they repent and are converted, shall have their sins pardoned, and be restored to God's favour.
[Deut.30.11-Deut.30.14]
Verses 11-14
The law is not too high for thee. It is not only known afar off; it is not confined to men of learning. It is written in thy books, made plain, so that he who runs may read it. It is in thy mouth, in the tongue commonly used by thee, in which thou mayest hear it read, and talk of it among thy children. It is delivered so that it is level to the understanding of the meanest. This is especially true of the gospel of Christ, to which the apostle applies it. But the word is nigh us, and Christ in that word; so that if we believe with the heart, that the promises of the Messiah are fulfilled in our Lord Jesus, and confess them with our mouth, we then have Christ with us.
[Deut.30.15-Deut.30.20]
Verses 15-20
What could be said more moving, and more likely to make deep and lasting impressions? Every man wishes to obtain life and good, and to escape death and evil; he desires happiness, and dreads misery. So great is the compassion of the Lord, that he has favoured men, by his word, with such a knowledge of good and evil as will make them for ever happy, if it be not their own fault. Let us hear the sum of the whole matter. If they and theirs would love God, and serve him, they should live and be happy. If they or theirs should turn from God, desert his service, and worship other gods, that would certainly be their ruin. There never was, since the fall of man, more than one way to heaven; which is marked out in both Testaments, though not with equal clearness. Moses meant that same way of acceptance, which Paul more plainly described; and Paul's words mean the same obedience, on which Moses more fully treated. In both Testaments the good and right way is brought near, and plainly revealed to us.
